The Case for Ending Prohibition: A Speech for Legalization, Regulation, and Taxation

Ladies and gentlemen,

I stand before you today to make a case that, at first hearing, may challenge you. It may unsettle you. Good. The most important ideas in American history have always unsettled people first—and liberated them after.

I am here to argue—passionately, unequivocally, and with evidence—that the United States should fully legalize, strictly regulate, and tax all drugs currently classified as illicit. Not because drugs are harmless. Not because addiction isn't devastating. But precisely because they are serious—too serious to be left to cartels, too serious to be managed by prisons, and too serious to be governed by stigma instead of science.

For over fifty years, we have run the largest social experiment in modern American history. We called it the War on Drugs. And by every measurable, honest standard—every single one—it has failed.

It is time for a new approach rooted in three principles I believe most Americans share: individual liberty, public health, and justice.

I. The Argument from Liberty

Let's begin where America itself began—with freedom.

This nation was founded on a radical premise: that individuals possess inherent rights, among them the right to make decisions about their own bodies and their own lives, so long as they do not directly harm others. We enshrine bodily autonomy in our medical decisions, in our reproductive choices, in our right to consume alcohol and tobacco—substances that kill hundreds of thousands of Americans every year.

And yet, if an adult chooses to consume a substance the government has placed on a different list—not because of some consistent scientific standard, but because of historical accident, racial panic, and political convenience—that adult can be stripped of their freedom, locked in a cage, and branded for life.

Let me be clear: I am not here to celebrate drug use. I am here to challenge the notion that the state has the moral authority to imprison people for what they choose to put into their own bodies. The philosopher John Stuart Mill wrote that "over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign." That principle does not come with an asterisk.

Alcohol prohibition taught us this lesson a century ago. Americans didn't stop drinking. They simply drank in the shadows—unregulated, dangerous, deadly bathtub gin—while organized crime grew rich and powerful. We repealed the Eighteenth Amendment not because we decided alcohol was good, but because we recognized prohibition was worse than the problem it aimed to solve.

We are living through the same lesson again. And we are paying for it in blood.

II. The Argument from Public Health

Now let me speak to those of you who are thinking: "But legalization would cause more addiction. More suffering. More death."

I hear you. That concern comes from a place of compassion. But I want to challenge you with a question: Compared to what?

Compared to what we have now?

Right now, over 100,000 Americans die of drug overdoses every year. One hundred thousand. That is more than car accidents, gun violence, and HIV combined. And that number has climbed—relentlessly, mercilessly—throughout five decades of prohibition.

Why? Because prohibition doesn't eliminate drugs. It eliminates quality control.

When you buy aspirin at a pharmacy, you know exactly what's in it, exactly how much to take, exactly what the risks are. When someone buys heroin or a pressed pill on the street, they are playing Russian roulette. They don't know the dose. They don't know the purity. They don't know if it's been laced with fentanyl or carfentanil. The leading driver of the overdose crisis is not that people use drugs—it's that people use unknown drugs in unknown doses with no medical guidance and no safety net.

Legalization with strict regulation changes that equation entirely.

Imagine a system—not unlike what we already have for alcohol and tobacco and, increasingly, cannabis—where substances are produced under pharmaceutical-grade standards. Where dosages are labeled. Where point-of-sale professionals can provide harm-reduction information. Where people who are struggling can seek help without fearing arrest. Where public health agencies can track usage patterns in real time and respond accordingly.

This is not fantasy. Portugal decriminalized all drugs in 2001. In the two decades since, they have seen dramatic reductions in overdose deaths, HIV infections among drug users, and drug-related crime—while usage rates remained comparable to or below the European average. Switzerland introduced prescription heroin programs in the 1990s for severe addicts. Crime among participants dropped by 60%. Employment doubled. Overdose deaths plummeted.

These examples involve decriminalization or medicalization—steps short of what I'm proposing. But they demonstrate a fundamental truth: when you treat drug use as a health issue rather than a criminal one, health outcomes improve.

Full legalization with regulation goes further. It doesn't just help the user. It destroys the poisoned, unpredictable black market that is the primary killer in this crisis.

Let me say that again: Prohibition does not protect people from drugs. It protects drugs from oversight.

We don't let people brew and sell unregulated whiskey out of garages. We don't let pharmaceutical companies sell unlabeled pills of random dosage. We regulate because regulation saves lives. The question is not whether drugs are dangerous. The question is whether we manage that danger with science—or surrender it to chaos.

III. The Argument from Social Justice

And now I must speak about the dimension of this issue that should haunt every American who believes in equality.

The War on Drugs has been, from its very inception, a war waged disproportionately against Black and Brown communities.

This is not a matter of opinion. It is documented, exposed, and confessed.

John Ehrlichman, domestic policy advisor to President Richard Nixon—the president who declared the War on Drugs—admitted it plainly in a 1994 interview published by Harper's Magazine. He said:

> "The Nixon campaign in 1968, and the Nixon White House after that, had two enemies: the antiwar left and Black people. You understand what I'm saying? We knew we couldn't make it illegal to be either against the war or Black, but by getting the public to associate the hippies with marijuana and Blacks with heroin, and then criminalizing both heavily, we could disrupt those communities."

That is not a conspiracy theory. That is the architect of the policy explaining its purpose.

And the machinery he helped build has operated with devastating efficiency ever since.

Black Americans and white Americans use drugs at roughly similar rates. Study after study confirms this. And yet, Black Americans are nearly four times more likely to be arrested for marijuana possession. They are incarcerated for drug offenses at nearly six times the rate of white Americans. In some jurisdictions, the disparity is even more grotesque.

The consequences cascade across generations. A drug conviction—even a minor one—can cost a person their right to vote, their access to public housing, their eligibility for student loans, their ability to get a job. We have created a permanent underclass, not through the effects of drugs themselves, but through the effects of criminalizing drugs.

We have spent over one trillion dollars on the War on Drugs since its inception. One trillion dollars—on a policy that has not reduced drug use, has not reduced addiction, has not reduced supply, but has torn apart families, destabilized communities, and filled the largest prison system in the history of the world.

The United States has 4% of the world's population and nearly 25% of the world's prisoners. Drug offenses are a leading driver of that staggering, shameful statistic.

Legalization does not just end this injustice going forward. Paired with the expungement of prior convictions and reinvestment of tax revenue into affected communities, it begins to repair it.

IV. The Economic Argument

Let me add a word about the practical economics, because policy must be sustainable.

The illegal drug market in the United States is estimated at tens of billions of dollars annually—some estimates range above $100 billion. Every dollar of that flows untaxed, unregulated, into the hands of criminal organizations, both domestic and international.

Legalization redirects that river of money.

It generates tax revenue—as cannabis legalization already has, producing billions of dollars across legal states, funding schools, treatment programs, and infrastructure.

It slashes law enforcement and incarceration costs. We spend roughly $50 billion a year on drug enforcement. Imagine that money redirected toward treatment, education, mental health services, and community development.

It defunds the cartels. The brutal transnational organizations that terrorize communities from Appalachia to Sinaloa exist because of prohibition. They are not selling a product people don't want. They are filling a demand that legal markets are forbidden from meeting. Remove prohibition, and you remove their business model—far more effectively than any interdiction operation ever has.

V. Regulation, Not Abdication

I want to address a concern I know many of you hold: "Legalization means a free-for-all. It means drugs sold to children. It means advertisements for methamphetamine on television."

No. Absolutely not. And I want to be emphatic about this.

Legalization means regulation. And regulation means rules—strict, enforceable, evidence-based rules.

We don't allow alcohol to be sold to minors. We don't allow tobacco to be advertised on television. We don't allow drivers to operate vehicles while intoxicated. Legalization of drugs would come with more control than currently exists in the black market, which has zero age verification, zero quality standards, zero dosage limits, and zero accountability.

Different substances would warrant different regulatory frameworks. Some might be available in controlled retail settings with mandatory education and dosage limits. Others—those with higher risk profiles—might be available only through licensed clinics or prescription models, as Switzerland has demonstrated with heroin-assisted treatment.

The point is that we would have tools. Right now, our only tools are handcuffs and prison cells—and they are not working.

VI. The Moral Summation

I'll close with this.

Every year, we lose a hundred thousand of our neighbors, our friends, our children—not because they used drugs, but because they used criminalized, unregulated drugs in a system that punished them for seeking help.

Every year, hundreds of thousands more are locked away, disproportionately poor, disproportionately Black and Brown, for choices that cause no direct harm to anyone else—while the substances that do kill the most Americans, alcohol and tobacco, are sold on every corner with legal protection.

Every year, billions of dollars flow to violent criminal enterprises because we have handed them a monopoly.

Every year, we choose punishment over compassion, ideology over evidence, fear over freedom.

I am not asking you to celebrate drugs. I am asking you to be honest about what prohibition has done and what it has failed to do. I am asking you to consider the possibility—supported by decades of evidence, endorsed by organizations from the American Civil Liberties Union to the Drug Policy Alliance to The Lancet—that there is a better way.

A way that respects the autonomy of adults. A way that protects the vulnerable through regulation, not incarceration. A way that treats addiction as the medical condition it is. A way that rights one of the most destructive racial injustices of our time. A way that replaces a failed war with a framework of safety, accountability, and compassion.

Prohibition has had fifty years to prove itself. It has proven only its capacity for destruction.

It is time to legalize. It is time to regulate. It is time to tax. It is time to invest in treatment, in communities, in science, and in each other.

It is time to end this war—not with surrender, but with wisdom.

Thank you.

Upholding Individual Liberty: The Right to Self-Determination

At the heart of American democracy is the unalienable right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. Yet, the prohibition of drugs like heroin, cocaine, and methamphetamine represents an egregious overreach by the government into the most personal realm: our own bodies. Why should the state dictate what substances adults can ingest, especially when safer alternatives like alcohol and tobacco—proven killers—are legally available? Legalization restores autonomy, allowing individuals to make informed choices about their own well-being without fear of imprisonment.

Consider the philosophical foundation of liberty espoused by thinkers like John Stuart Mill in On Liberty, where he argues that the only justification for limiting personal freedom is to prevent harm to others. The current system, by contrast, punishes personal choices with devastating consequences. At the heart of the argument for drug legalization lies the fundamental principle of individual liberty, a cornerstone of American democracy enshrined in the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. The complete prohibition of drugs in the United States has failed by every metric by which a policy should be judged. It has failed to prevent use, failed to reduce supply, failed to protect public health, and failed to uphold the principles of individual liberty on which this country was founded. It is time to replace this failed model with a policy rooted in reality, responsibility, and reason: the complete legalization, strict regulation, and taxation of all currently illicit drugs, including heroin, cocaine, and methamphetamine.

The case for legalization rests on three pillars: individual liberty, harm reduction, and economic pragmatism.

1. Individual Liberty and the Limits of Government Power

The philosophical foundation of the United States is the idea that adults own their own bodies and minds. The government exists to protect us from harming others, not to protect us from ourselves.

If an adult can legally consume alcohol - a substance that contributes to over 95,000 deaths per year, fuels domestic violence, and is highly addictive - smoke tobacco, eat a diet that causes heart disease, and own a firearm, then the principle that government can criminalize the private chemical choices of that same adult is inconsistent and paternalistic.

Criminalization turns a matter of personal health and autonomy into a felony. We do not arrest people for self-destructive behavior; we counsel them, we treat them, we try to help them. A heroin addict needs medical help, housing support, and treatment, not a prison cell that will strip him of his job, his right to vote, his eligibility for student loans and public housing, and brand him a felon for life. Legalization does not mean endorsement. It means recognizing that in a free society, the state does not have the moral authority to dictate what an adult puts into his or her own body, provided that person does not infringe on the rights of others.

2. Harm Reduction: Regulation Makes Drugs Safer

The core fallacy of prohibition is that it makes drugs go away. It does not. It makes drugs more dangerous.

Today, there is no such thing as an illicit drug market - there is a market for unknown chemicals sold as drugs. When heroin is banned, it is not produced in clean, regulated labs with accurate dosages. It is produced in clandestine labs and cut with levamisole, fentanyl, and other lethal adulterants. The explosion of overdose deaths in America - over 100,000 per year - is not primarily an overdose crisis caused by heroin or cocaine. It is a poisoning crisis caused by prohibition. People are dying because they do not know what they are taking or how strong it is.

Legalization solves this through regulation, exactly as we did after the disaster of alcohol Prohibition in the 1920s.

Under a legal, regulated system:

  • Purity and dosage would be standardized. A person buying cocaine or heroin from a licensed dispensary would receive a product of known purity, in a measured dose, with clear labeling and warnings, just like whiskey or prescription opioids.
  • Transmission of disease would plummet. HIV and Hepatitis C spread rapidly through shared, dirty needles. A legal system would eliminate the need for needle-sharing and could provide clean supplies and safe-use education.
  • Addiction would be treated as a medical issue, not a criminal one. When drugs are legal, people who struggle with problematic use are far more likely to seek help. They don't fear arrest. Portugal, which decriminalized all drugs in 2001, saw dramatic drops in overdose deaths, HIV infection rates, and drug use among adolescents. Switzerland's legal heroin-assisted treatment program took chronic addicts off the streets, gave them pharmaceutical-grade heroin in a clinical setting, and as a result reduced overdose deaths by 50%, cut crime, and helped the majority gain employment and stable housing.
  • The incentive for more potent drugs disappears. Just as alcohol prohibition created a market for highly potent moonshine and bootleg spirits, drug prohibition created crack and fentanyl - drugs that are easier to smuggle because they are stronger in smaller amounts. A legal market brings users back to less potent, less risky forms.

We cannot make drugs safe, but we can make them vastly safer than they are today. Prohibition maximizes harm. Regulation minimizes it.

3. The Economic and Public Safety Case

The War on Drugs is the most expensive failed policy in American history. Since 1971, we have spent over $1 trillion directly fighting drug enforcement. We spend over $50 billion every year on police, DEA agents, courts, and prisons for drug offenses.

What do we get for that money? Cartels with annual revenues larger than the GDP of many countries, who murder tens of thousands in Mexico and Central America to control smuggling routes into the U.S. We get street gangs whose primary funding comes from drug profits. We get the militarization of police and the erosion of Fourth Amendment rights through no-knock raids and civil asset forfeiture.

Legalization would bankrupt these organizations overnight. No cartel ever formed to smuggle alcohol after Prohibition ended. No gang controls the tobacco trade.

Consider the economic upside:

  • Tax Revenue: If taxed at a rate similar to alcohol and tobacco, legal drugs could generate tens of billions of dollars annually. A 2010 Cato Institute and Harvard study estimated that legalizing all drugs would save the federal government $41.3 billion in enforcement costs and generate up to $46.7 billion in tax revenue - a combined $88 billion swing. That money could be earmarked, by law, for treatment, education, and prevention programs that actually work.
  • Law Enforcement Resources: Every hour a detective spends on a drug possession case is an hour not spent investigating rape, murder, robbery, or child exploitation. Legalization would allow us to reallocate police, prosecutors, and prisons to violent and property crime.
  • Workforce and Productivity: Instead of warehousing 400,000 people for non-violent drug offenses, keeping them unemployed and unemployable, we would keep them in the taxpaying workforce and with their families.

Opponents will argue that legalization would send the wrong message and cause drug use to skyrocket. The evidence says otherwise. Addiction rates have remained remarkably constant throughout American history, under both prohibition and legal regimes. Use does not appear or disappear based on its legal status; it is driven by trauma, mental health, poverty, social isolation, and genetics. Legalization does not create addicts. It simply decides how we treat them - as patients or as prisoners.

No one wants a nation of addicts. But we already live in one, because prohibition has not prevented addiction. We have a choice between an illegal market that promotes death, disease, cartel violence, and mass incarceration, and a legal market that promotes order, safety, transparency, and treatment.

We have tried punishment for over 50 years. It is time to try common sense. Legalize, regulate, and tax all drugs.
